author: cskiraly
content:
As you say, Waggle is a base protocol. It can be a good fit for almost everything because it is a common base abstraction layer. It is a naming convention, and the conceptual model behind that naming convention, mostly. Even that is still to be tested because it still misses a refined specification, but that's AFAIK on the way, and that's a good thing. What it does not define is the use case specific protocol logic sitting on top. That's actually part of the waggle thesis: it does not want to specify that.  

To illustrate it better also to those less into networking stacks, here are some analogies that I hope will make this clear:
- "we agreed to use UDP, why are we speaking of Waggle. "
- "we agreed to use IP, why are we discussing UDP"
- " we agreed to use ....
Once upon a time, There was no IP and TCP defined separately. It was one mess of a protocol. Then people realised it helps to separate those two, and they stand on their own. That doesn't make IP solve all our networking needs.

Similarly, Waggle has its stated goals of being that base layer. The agreement you mention was on trying to have this common base vocabulary and layer defined and used. I don't think we can see more into it. In fact this was explicitly discussed in that specific meeting. 

Yet, as uncomfortable as it is, interoperable networking protocols are slightly more complex than just a base layer, or saying that we have topics that have names and pieces that we exchange. Seacast is an attempt to map out and solve that complexity. The part waggle does not try to solve.
